extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claimed subject matter is patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, including identifying the closest natural counterpart, selecting characteristics for comparison (markedly different analysis), and performing the Alice/Mayo Step 2B inventive-concept inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the closest natural counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing a nature-based product claim to something in nature, the examiner should compare the claimed product to the closest naturally occurring counterpart (e.g., an isolated gene should be compared to the gene itself, not the whole chromosome).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and guidance: compare an isolated nucleic acid to the naturally occurring gene sequence (Ass’n for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics, Inc.); compare a single-stranded primer to the corresponding sense strand even if the natural molecule is double-stranded (University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics). When multiple natural counterparts exist (e.g., cloned animal made from DNA of two breeds), select the counterpart most closely related based on examiner expertise (Roslin). For combinations produced from multiple components, the closest counterparts may be the individual nature-based components (Funk Bros.; Ambry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action practice: identify selected counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is rejected as ineligible, it is a 'best practice' for the examiner to identify the selected counterpart in the Office action if the record is not already clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice assists the applicant in responding and clarifies how the examiner is interpreting the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics chosen for the markedly different analysis must be possessed by the claimed product because the claim must define the invention to be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners identify such characteristics by looking at what is recited in the claim and what is encompassed within the broadest reasonable interpretation (e.g., a claim to 'deoxyribose' conveys structural characteristics; a claim to 'isolated gene B' requires reliance on BRI to determine sequence or encoded protein). Unclaimed characteristics cannot contribute to eligibility (Roslin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of characteristics to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate characteristics can be expressed as the nature-based product’s structure, function, and/or other properties, evaluated case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting types considered by courts include: biological or pharmacological functions or activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype (functional/structural characteristics); and structure and form (chemical, genetic, or physical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological or pharmacological function examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Biological or pharmacological functions or activities are relevant characteristics when assessing marked differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include protein-encoding information of a nucleic acid (Myriad), ability of complementary nucleotide sequences to bind (Ambry), properties/functions of bacteria like infecting certain plants (Funk Bros.), ability to degrade hydrocarbons (Chakrabarty), and biological activity such as vitamin C preventing scurvy (In re King).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical and physical property examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical and physical properties can be appropriate characteristics for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include alkalinity of a compound (Parke-Davis) and ductility/malleability of metals (In re Marden).

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenotypic characteristic examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenotypic characteristics (functional and structural) may be considered in the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include shape, size, color, and behavior of an organism (Roslin). Note that unclaimed phenotypic differences generally cannot make a claimed subject matter markedly different if they are not claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and form examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure and form—physical, chemical, genetic—are relevant characteristics to compare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: physical presence of plasmids in a bacterial cell (Chakrabarty); chemical state such as 'nonsalt' or 'crystalline substance' (Parke-Davis); nucleotide sequence of DNA (Myriad); genetic makeup (genotype) of a cell or organism (Roslin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristic requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a marked difference, a characteristic must be changed as compared to nature and cannot be an inherent/innate characteristic of the naturally occurring counterpart or an incidental change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic that is different from that of the counterpart; if there is no change, the claimed product is a product of nature exception. If there is a change that was produced by applicant’s efforts, the change will generally be considered markedly different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products having markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Court-identified examples where claimed nature-based products had markedly different characteristics and were eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chakrabarty: genetically modified bacterium that could degrade multiple hydrocarbons and contained additional plasmids (changed function and structure) — eligible. Myriad: cDNA that retained exons but had different nucleotide sequence (lacking introns) — eligible as distinct from naturally occurring DNA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products lacking markedly different characteristics (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court examples where claimed products lacked marked differences and were held products of nature (ineligible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad: isolated genes that differed only by isolation (missing covalent bonds) but otherwise identical nucleotide sequence — not markedly different. Ambry: single-stranded primers with same nucleotide sequence and innate primer function — not markedly different. Marden: ductility of vanadium was inherent and not conferred by combination — ineligible. Roslin: clones genetically identical to donors lacked markedly different characteristics; alleged phenotypic differences were not claimed and thus could not confer eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Search for an inventive concept (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: After determining a claim is directed to a judicial exception, the search for an 'inventive concept' asks whether additional claim elements amount to 'significantly more' than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventive concept cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea itself; it is furnished by an element or combination recited in the claim in addition to the judicial exception (Alice; Mayo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating whether additional elements provide an inventive concept requires considering those elements both individually and as an ordered combination to ensure the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consideration in combination is important because elements that are conventional individually may amount to significantly more when arranged non-conventionally (Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect; BASCOM). The claim must be considered as a whole (Diamond v. Diehr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept distinct from novelty/non-obviousness (§102/103)
rubrics_metrics.description: The search for an inventive concept is a distinct inquiry from novelty (§102) and obviousness (§103) and should not be conflated with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have rejected substituting §§ 102/103 inquiries for §101 eligibility; novelty or non-obviousness of elements is of no relevance in determining §101 eligibility (Mayo; Diamond v. Diehr; Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics). Conversely, patentability under §§ 102/103 does not guarantee §101 eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that have qualified as 'significantly more' (non-exhaustive list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of additional limitations have been found by courts to qualify as 'significantly more' when recited with a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court-identified qualifying limitations include: (i) improvements to the functioning of a computer (DDR Holdings); (ii) improvements to any other technology or technical field (Diehr); (iii) applying the judicial exception with, or by use of, a particular machine arranged in a specific way (Eibel Process); (iv) effecting a transformation or reduction of an article to a different state or thing (Diehr); (v) adding a specific limitation beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (BASCOM); and (vi) other meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment (e.g., an immunization step integrating data comparison into a specific process) (Classen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that do NOT qualify as 'significantly more' (anti-pattern list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain added limitations have been held insufficient to supply an inventive concept when coupled with a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court-identified non-qualifying limitations include: (i) adding the words 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (Alice); (ii) appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality (Alice; BASCOM discussion); (iii) adding insignificant extra-solution activity such as mere data gathering (CyberSource); and (iv) generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (Bilski; Parker v. Flook). See MPEP § 2106.05(f)-(h) for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere physicality or tangibility is not enough
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere physical or tangible implementation of a judicial exception (e.g., reciting a computer) is not, by itself, an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court explained that physicality/tangibility of a computer is 'beside the point' because allowing such claims would let applicants claim any principle by reciting a computer system configured to implement it, thus making eligibility depend on 'the draftsman’s art' (Alice). Mere recitation of a machine does not guarantee eligibility.
